A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ODE-GS and retain the same foundational framework and overlapping experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–B and supplementary figures and tables were included.

before.justification: v1 reports original ODE-GS extrapolation results on D-NeRF and NVFI, including numerical comparisons in Tables 1–2 and qualitative results in Figure 2.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on D-NeRF, NVFi, and HyperNeRF, plus component ablations, deterministic-versus-variational comparisons, and a multi-scene generalization experiment.

M1.justification: v2 makes the existing deterministic variant the primary model while retaining variational forecasting in Appendix A.0.2. More substantively, it adds Gaussian-position acceleration regularization and EMA-controlled adaptive regularization weighting to v1's fixed-weight latent smoothness penalty. Dynamic prefix–suffix sampling already exists in v1; its expanded description alone is not a new component.

E1.justification: v2 expands synthetic-only evaluation to six real-world HyperNeRF scenes and adds fallingball to the NVFi evaluation. Appendix B.2 introduces a distinct transfer scenario: a forecaster trained jointly on other NVFi scenes is tested on withheld whale trajectories, using whale's separately fitted interpolation model.

E2.justification: The four external comparators on the original benchmarks are retained. v2 adds NVFi itself to the NVFi benchmark comparison and introduces a pure autoregressive Transformer control. The deterministic-versus-variational comparison disappears from D-NeRF Table 1 and is newly reported on NVFi in Table 5, rather than merely relocating the same experiment.

E3.justification: The reported training recipe changes from 20 context/20 target points and a 0.3 context span to lengths of 30/10 and spans of 0.6 for D-NeRF and 0.5 for NVFi. Learning-rate and regularization settings also change. v2 adds HyperNeRF's 90/10 temporal split and shared-forecaster training with whale withheld; existing D-NeRF 80/20 and NVFi 75/25 splits remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's deterministic/variational comparison, v2 adds controlled removal of the ODE, regularizers, adaptive weighting, and dynamic sampling, with averages and per-scene results in Tables 4, 6, and 7. Figure 4 visualizes regularization effects. Appendix B.2/Table 8 additionally tests joint training and transfer to withheld scene dynamics.

E5.justification: Both versions report point metrics and scene averages without seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. Their descriptions of probabilistic latent states do not provide empirical uncertainty estimates for the reported benchmark results.

E6.justification: v1 reports D-NeRF average PSNR of 26.53 for deterministic and 27.01 for variational ODE-GS; v2 reports 27.30 for its revised deterministic model. NVFi variational results are substantially replaced: bat PSNR changes from 38.50 to 28.01. TiNeuVox's telescope PSNR changes from 24.04 to 27.04. HyperNeRF, ablation, and multi-scene results are added. Changed training recipes and coverage preclude treating these collectively as same-setting gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for positional acceleration regularization, the combined training objective, and EMA-based adaptive scaling in Equations 7–11. Existing latent-ODE and variational mathematics is largely retained or relocated. Neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs; the additions concern limited objective and weighting definitions.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds variational forecasting and claims state-of-the-art extrapolation on two synthetic benchmarks. v2 centers smoothness-prior modeling, explicitly claims benefits from regularizing both latent and decoded trajectories, and extends its state-of-the-art claim to real-world HyperNeRF. Its abstract and contribution list also replace the earlier gain summaries with aggregate percentage claims.

C2.justification: v1 motivates variational inference through uncertain futures and the shortcomings of deterministic averaging. v2 instead attributes poor variational NVFi results to sampling/KL optimization difficulties and underfitting. Section 5 adds substantive limitations involving interpolation-error propagation, fast small objects, abrupt dynamics, and unforeseeable behavior. Appendix B.2 qualifies cross-scene generalization as preliminary and generally weaker than per-scene training.

D1.justification: v2 adds sinusoidal positional-encoding disclosure, explicit trajectory-sampling formulas, a 40,000-iteration interpolation schedule, and temperature, EMA, and adaptive-regularization settings. Most architecture, solver, tolerance, and hardware details are retained and moved to Appendix B.1. Conversely, v1's variational noise scale and KL-annealing schedule are no longer specified for the retained variational comparison.

R1.justification: The central positioning around Gaussian splatting and latent ODEs remains. v2 explicitly discusses NVFi as an extrapolation predecessor and drops v1's assertion of being the only continuous-time scene-prediction work. It adds human-prediction, Transformer, VAE, HyperNeRF, and LPIPS references while pruning portions of the efficient-rendering and ODE-variant literature.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around underconstrained prediction and smoothness priors. The method presentation is reorganized, related-work subsections become compact topical paragraphs, implementation and dataset details move into appendices, and the conclusion gains a limitations discussion. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds an interpolation/extrapolation schematic, redraws the workflow, expands qualitative comparisons from one D-NeRF scene to five plus five NVFi scenes, and adds a regularization visualization. Benchmark tables are reorganized into scene blocks with method rows and colored rankings. New benchmark, ablation, variant-comparison, and transfer tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the method through real-video evaluation, the relevant NVFi comparator, and controlled component ablations that address important gaps in v1. Explicit failure conditions and the qualified transfer experiment also improve scientific interpretation. Reporting weaknesses remain: the variational-score revisions lack a clear cross-version explanation, and the claimed chickchicken PSNR lead contradicts Table 3's 20.29 versus GaussianPredict's 21.94. Nevertheless, the added diagnostic evidence and applicability boundaries provide a substantial net quality improvement.
